## SECTION 2: Statement of Need (~600 words)

**Rubric:** Need/Community Impact (30%): clarity of problem, target population, data

### Draft

> **Statement of Need**
>
> Reading proficiency by the end of third grade is one of the strongest predictors of a child's long-term success. Students who are not reading proficiently by third grade are four times more likely to leave high school without a diploma than proficient readers (Hernandez, *Double Jeopardy*, Annie E. Casey Foundation, 2011). Third grade marks the shift from *learning to read* to *reading to learn*. Children who haven't made that shift fall further behind in every subject.
>
> **The problem in Westside County.** In Westside County, 42% of third graders read below grade level ([State] Department of Education, [assessment name], [school year]), compared with [X]% statewide. This rate has [risen / remained above X%] since [year], when [baseline]% of third graders were below grade level, indicating a persistent gap rather than a one-year dip.
>
> The warning signs appear well before third grade. In fall [year], [X]% of Westside kindergartners and [X]% of first graders scored below benchmark on [DIBELS / MAP Growth / district screener] ([Westside County School District], [year]). Without targeted support, early gaps in phonemic awareness, phonics, and fluency tend to widen over time.
>
> **Where the need is concentrated.** The need is most acute at [School A], [School B], and [School C]. At these schools, [X]% of K–3 students read below benchmark and [X]% qualify for free or reduced-price meals ([source, year]). In the surrounding neighborhoods, [X]% of children under 18 live below the poverty line, and [X]% of households speak a language other than English at home (U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates, [years]).
>
> **Why students are falling behind.** Teachers in Westside's K–3 classrooms serve an average of [X] students each ([source]). That leaves limited time for the individualized practice that struggling early readers need. The district employs [X] reading interventionists for [X] K–3 students, a ratio of roughly 1:[X] ([district source]). As a result, [X] students identified for reading intervention are currently [on a waitlist / receiving less than the recommended support] ([source]).
>
> At home, families want to help but often lack the tools. In our [year] survey of [n] Westside parents, [X]% said they wanted to support their child's reading but [X]% were unsure how. [X]% reported having fewer than [X] children's books at home ([Literacy Lift parent survey, year]). Research shows that when parents are taught specific strategies to support reading, children's literacy skills improve more than when parents simply read aloud (Sénéchal & Young, *Review of Educational Research*, 2008).
>
> **Gaps in existing services.** Current reading support in Westside County is limited. [Existing program, if any] serves [grades/sites] but does not reach [gap]. No program currently pairs individual tutoring with family literacy instruction for K–3 students at [target schools]. Teachers and principals have asked for additional support. [Principal name/title] notes, "[quote about need]" (letter of support attached).
>
> **Why now.** [If local data support it:] Westside's early-grade reading scores have not returned to pre-2020 levels. The students who are in K–3 today are the ones who will reach the third-grade benchmark in the next [1–4] years. Intervening now, while these students are still learning foundational skills, is significantly more effective and less costly than remediation in later grades.
>
> Literacy Lift will serve **120 K–3 students** reading below grade level at [target schools], along with their families. By combining weekly one-on-one tutoring with family literacy workshops, we address both causes of the gap: too little individualized practice at school, and too few tools at home.

## SECTION 4: Program Design & Activities (~800 words)

**Rubric:** Program Design & Activities (30%): logic, timeline, staffing

### Draft

> **Program Design & Activities**
>
> **Overview and theory of change.** Literacy Lift addresses Westside County's early reading gap through two linked components:
>
> 1. **Weekly one-on-one tutoring** gives struggling readers the individualized, structured practice they can't get in a full classroom.
> 2. **Monthly family literacy workshops** equip parents to reinforce those skills at home.
>
> Our theory of change is straightforward. Students who receive consistent, skill-targeted practice at school and at home will build foundational reading skills faster, leading to measurable gains in reading achievement (see Logic Model, Attachment [X]).
>
> **Component 1: One-on-One Tutoring**
>
> *What:* Each of 120 K–3 students is matched with a trained volunteer tutor for weekly 45-minute sessions over 30 weeks, from [October] through [May]. That totals up to 22.5 hours of individualized instruction per student.
>
> *Curriculum:* Tutors follow [curriculum name], a structured, sequenced program aligned with the science of reading. It targets phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension. Each session follows a consistent format:
> - Review of a known skill (10 min)
> - Explicit instruction in a new skill (15 min)
> - Guided reading in a leveled text (15 min)
> - Wrap-up and a take-home activity (5 min)
>
> *Where and when:* Sessions take place [during the school day / in an after-school block] at [target schools], in space provided by each school. Times are coordinated with teachers so that students don't miss core literacy instruction.
>
> *Matching and individualization:* Each student's starting point is set using fall MAP Growth scores and a brief diagnostic. The Program Coordinator uses these to place the student in the curriculum sequence. Tutors record progress after every session. Every [4–6] weeks, the Coordinator reviews progress data and adjusts each student's plan.
>
> *Tutor recruitment and training:* We will recruit [X] volunteers from [local colleges, retiree networks, faith communities, corporate partners]. Each tutor commits to [one or two] students for the full school year. Before their first session, every tutor completes:
> - [X] hours of initial training in the curriculum, early literacy fundamentals, and child safety
> - A background check
>
> Throughout the year, tutors receive ongoing support through monthly refresher sessions and on-site observation by the Program Coordinator.
>
> *Retention:* To keep volunteers engaged and consistent, we provide [recognition events, flexible scheduling, a substitute tutor pool]. Last year, [X]% of our tutors completed their full commitment.
>
> **Component 2: Family Literacy Workshops**
>
> *What:* We will hold eight monthly 90-minute workshops at [location], open to families of all enrolled students. Each workshop teaches one or two concrete at-home strategies that match what students are practicing with their tutors. Topics include:
> - Sounding out words together
> - Asking questions during read-alouds
> - Building a daily reading routine
>
> *Format:* Each workshop includes:
> - A brief demonstration
> - Guided parent-child practice
> - Take-home materials: books for the home library, activity cards, and a reading log
>
> *Access:* To reduce barriers, we provide dinner, childcare for siblings, and interpretation in [languages]. Workshops are offered at [two times / in person and recorded] to accommodate working families.
>
> *Evidence base:* Teaching parents specific literacy strategies produces stronger child outcomes than encouraging general reading alone (Sénéchal & Young, 2008). Aligning workshop content with tutoring reinforces skills across settings.
>
> **Participant Pathway**
>
> 1. **Identification (Sept):** Teachers and reading specialists refer K–3 students scoring [below the 40th percentile on fall MAP / below benchmark on the district screener].
> 2. **Enrollment (Sept–Oct):** Families provide consent. This includes data-sharing permission for assessment scores.
> 3. **Services (Oct–May):** Students receive weekly tutoring, and families attend monthly workshops.
> 4. **Progress monitoring:** Tutors keep session logs, and the Coordinator reviews progress every [4–6] weeks.
> 5. **Exit (May–June):** We review spring MAP scores, share an end-of-year family report, and provide summer reading packets.
>
> **Evidence for our approach.** Meta-analyses show that structured tutoring improves early reading outcomes, including when delivered by trained volunteers (Ritter et al., *Review of Educational Research*, 2009; Nickow, Oreopoulos & Quan, 2020). Effects are strongest in the early grades and when tutors follow a structured curriculum. Literacy Lift is built on both findings.
>
> **Implementation.** The program is managed by a [0.X FTE] Program Coordinator, who handles student matching, tutor training and supervision, and data collection. A [Family Engagement Lead / workshop facilitator] runs the workshops. Each partner school designates a liaison to coordinate referrals and scheduling. (See Section 5: Staffing & Timeline.)

### Additional phrasing hooks
- "Every activity responds directly to a barrier identified in our Statement of Need."
- "At $400 per student, Literacy Lift delivers 22.5 hours of individualized instruction plus family support." This one is useful for the Budget section too.
- "Tutoring builds skills at school; workshops sustain them at home."

## Evidence to Gather (Checklist)

- [ ] Source and year for the 42% figure, plus the statewide comparison
- [ ] 3–5 years of trend data for the same measure
- [ ] K–2 screener data from the district
- [ ] School-level FRL and demographics for target schools
- [ ] ACS child poverty and home-language data for the target area
- [ ] Interventionist ratio and waitlist numbers from the district
- [ ] Parent survey results (run a quick one if you don't have one)
- [ ] Inventory of existing literacy programs in the county, to show the service gap
- [ ] Letters of support from principals and the district
- [ ] Curriculum name and documentation
- [ ] Past tutor retention rates and student results, if you have them
- [ ] Signed MOU and data-sharing agreement with the district

---

## ⚠️ Weak Spots & Assumptions to Verify

**High priority. Reviewers are likely to catch these:**

1. **The 42% statistic needs a source, year, and definition.** Is it the state test ("not proficient") or MAP ("below grade level")? These are different measures. Use the exact language your source uses.
2. **Your statistic covers 3rd grade only, but you serve K–3.** Without K–2 data, reviewers may question the need in younger grades. Get district screener data.
3. **Dosage is low.** Research on high-impact tutoring generally points to 3+ sessions per week. Once-weekly volunteer tutoring tends to show smaller effects. Your options:
   - Move to two 30-minute sessions per week, if your volunteer capacity allows
   - Keep weekly sessions, but explicitly justify them by pointing to the structured curriculum, the family component multiplying practice time, and the take-home activities
4. **Volunteer capacity is unproven in the draft.** 120 students means 60–120 committed volunteers. Reviewers will ask how you'll recruit and retain them. Cite past numbers if you have them.
5. **MAP data access is assumed.** The district administers MAP, so you need a data-sharing agreement and parental consent (FERPA). Confirm this before you promise it as your outcome measure.

**Medium priority:**

6. **Student selection criteria aren't defined.** Specify the cutoff, such as below the 40th percentile or below benchmark.
7. **Fall kindergarten MAP scores can be less reliable.** Consider a supplementary early literacy screener for K students.
8. **Tutoring during school vs. after school.** Pulling students from class requires teacher buy-in. After-school sessions affect attendance. Name which one, and confirm it with the schools.
9. **Home-reading frequency will be self-reported.** That's fine, but acknowledge it in the Evaluation section and describe the tool (reading logs, parent survey).
10. **Workshop attendance assumptions.** Parent workshops often see low turnout. Set a realistic target, such as 50–60% of families attending at least half the workshops, and keep the access supports in the design.
11. **Citations.** I've referenced well-known studies, but pull and confirm each one before submitting. Check that the findings are described accurately.

**A strength to play up:** $400 per student is very cost-effective for 22.5 instructional hours plus family support. That will help in the Budget section, as long as the budget realistically covers coordinator time, training, materials, and background checks.

---

**Next up, when you're ready:** Section 3 (Target Population, ~300 words) and Section 5 (Staffing & Timeline). Those also feed the 30% Need and 30% Design scores. Or tell me which numbers you've already got, and I'll plug them in.

### Draft

> **Target Population**
>
> Literacy Lift will serve **120 kindergarten through third-grade students** each year at three Westside County elementary schools: [School A], [School B], and [School C]. We will also serve their families. These schools have the county's highest concentrations of early readers below benchmark ([X]%, [X]%, and [X]% of K–3 students; [district screener, year]). They also have the highest rates of students qualifying for free or reduced-price meals ([X]–[X]%; [source, year]).
>
> **Eligibility.** Students are eligible if they meet two conditions:
> 1. They are enrolled in grades K–3 at a partner school.
> 2. They score below benchmark on the district's fall K–3 reading screener, [name], which is approximately the bottom 40% of students.
>
> Students who receive intensive (Tier 3) intervention or have IEP reading goals are also eligible. Their intervention team must confirm that tutoring will complement their existing services rather than replace them.
>
> **Prioritization.** An estimated [X] students across the three schools meet the cutoff, far more than our 120 slots. We will prioritize students with the lowest screener scores. We will also prioritize those whose families report limited home literacy resources on a brief intake questionnaire, such as fewer than [10] children's books at home or no regular reading routine. Eligible students who are not enrolled will join a waitlist and fill slots as they open.
>
> **Who they are.** We expect participants to reflect their schools' demographics. Approximately [X]% will come from low-income households, and [X]% will be English learners ([source, year]). Each school will enroll 40 students, distributed across grades K–3.
>
> **Enrollment and consent.** Teachers and reading specialists refer students based on screener results. Families then provide written consent, available in [languages], for two things: participation in the program, and release of specified assessment records to Literacy Lift, consistent with FERPA. No student data is shared until consent is on file.

### Eligibility & Verification Protocol (for your internal use or an attachment)

| Step | What happens | Who | Documentation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Screening | District administers the fall screener. The school identifies students below benchmark or the cutoff. | School/district | Screener report (stays with the school until consent) |
| 2. Referral | Teacher or reading specialist refers eligible students and flags any Tier 3 or IEP students | School liaison | Referral form |
| 3. Family outreach | School sends the program invitation and consent packet in the home language | School + Literacy Lift | Translated packet |
| 4. Consent | Parent signs (a) a participation consent and (b) a FERPA records-release consent | Parent | Signed forms, filed securely |
| 5. Intake | Parent completes the home literacy questionnaire (used for prioritization and baseline) | Literacy Lift | Intake form |
| 6. Prioritization | Rank by screener score plus home literacy indicators; enroll 40 per school and waitlist the rest | Coordinator + liaison | Enrollment roster and waitlist |
| 7. Data transfer | District shares scores for consented students only, under the DSA | District → Coordinator | Secure transfer log |

**FERPA consent must specify** (34 CFR §99.30):
- Which records will be shared (e.g., fall, winter, and spring screener and MAP scores)
- The purpose (program placement and evaluation)
- Who will receive them (Literacy Lift)
- A signature and date

Pair the consent with a **district data-sharing agreement** that covers storage, access limits, retention and destruction, and breach notification. Some districts instead designate partners as "school officials" or use the studies exception. Ask which approach your district uses, but parental consent is the safest default.

- [ ] School-level K–3 below-benchmark rates (district assessment office)

- [ ] The district's exact screener name and its benchmark definition
- [ ] District consent template or DSA template (ask before writing your own)
- [ ] Draft home literacy intake questionnaire (5–8 items)

### Phrasing Hooks

- "Eligibility is based on objective screener data, not subjective referral alone."
- "No student data is shared without written family consent."

# Outcomes, Evaluation & Budget: Expanded Draft

Brackets are placeholders, and **no Westside County figures are verified.** Dollar figures are illustrative estimates for you to replace with your actual salaries, quotes, and rates.

**First, the risk flags that got cut off last time (Target Population & Staffing):**
- **Fix the 120-student math** (3 × 40, or 4 × 30) everywhere.
- **The district's fall screener must happen early enough.** If results arrive in late September, enrollment slips and tutoring starts later than October 1. Confirm the screening window.
- **Background check turnaround** (2–6 weeks for fingerprinting in some states) could delay the start.
- **A 0.6 FTE coordinator for 3 schools and 80+ tutors is a stretch.** Volunteer Site Leads help, but be ready to defend this ratio.
- **School space and schedule (in-school vs. after-school) must be confirmed in writing** before submitting.
- **Ask whether Tier 3/IEP students can receive outside tutoring.** Some districts restrict this.

---

## SECTION 6: Outcomes & Objectives (~400 words)

**Rubric:** Outcomes & Evaluation (20%), specifically measurable outcomes and baseline

### Draft

> **Outcomes & Objectives**
>
> Literacy Lift's goal is to help K–3 students reading below benchmark build the foundational skills they need to read proficiently by the end of third grade. We will track three participant outcomes and one implementation objective. Each has a baseline and a measurable target.
>
> **Objective 1: Reading growth.** By May 31, [20XX], at least **60%** of participants who complete 24 or more of 30 tutoring sessions will meet or exceed their individual fall-to-spring growth projection on NWEA MAP Growth Reading.
> - *Baseline:* MAP growth projections are set at the national median, so about 50% of students meet them in a typical year. Last year, [X]% of below-benchmark K–3 students at our partner schools met their projection ([district, year]).
>
> **Objective 2: Benchmark movement.** By May 31, at least **35%** of participants will advance at least one risk category on the district screener, [name] (for example, from "well below benchmark" to "below benchmark," or from "below" to "at or above benchmark").
